questions.question_text:
Mia scored $81$ in Art, where the mean was $72$ and the standard deviation was $12$.
She scored $58$ in Music, where the mean was $50$ and the standard deviation was $8$.
In which subject was her result better relative to the class?

options.text: Music, because its $z$-score of $1$ is higher than the Art $z$-score of $0.75$
Art, because $81$ is the higher mark
options.why: Compares raw marks from two different tests, which have different means and different spreads.

options.text: Art, because it is $9$ marks above its mean while Music is only $8$ marks above
options.why: Compares the raw differences $x - \mu$ without dividing by each standard deviation.

options.text: Equally well, because both marks are above their means
options.why: Treats 'above the mean' as a single category instead of measuring how far above in standard deviations.

questions.solution_text:
Art: $z = \dfrac{81 - 72}{12}$
$= 0.75$
Music: $z = \dfrac{58 - 50}{8}$
$= 1$
$1 > 0.75$, so her Music result was better relative to the class, even though Art was the higher mark.

questions.question_text:
Lachlan swims $50$ m freestyle in $31.2$ s, where the club mean is $34.0$ s with a standard deviation of $1.4$ s. He swims $50$ m breaststroke in $39.6$ s, where the club mean is $43.2$ s with a standard deviation of $2.4$ s. A faster (lower) time is better.
In which event was his swim better relative to the club?

options.text: Freestyle, because its $z$-score of $-2$ is further below the mean than the breaststroke $z$-score of $-1.5$
Breaststroke, because $-1.5$ is greater than $-2$
options.why: Applies the higher-z-score rule when a low value is better; for times the more negative z-score wins.

options.text: Breaststroke, because $3.6$ s below the club mean beats $2.8$ s below
options.why: Compares the raw differences without dividing by each standard deviation.

options.text: Breaststroke, because its standard deviation is larger
options.why: Reads the size of the standard deviation as a measure of performance rather than as the scale used to standardise.

questions.solution_text:
Freestyle: $z = \dfrac{31.2 - 34.0}{1.4}$
$= \dfrac{-2.8}{1.4}$
$= -2$
Breaststroke: $z = \dfrac{39.6 - 43.2}{2.4}$
$= \dfrac{-3.6}{2.4}$
$= -1.5$
A lower time is better here, so the more negative $z$-score is the better swim.
$-2 < -1.5$, so his freestyle swim was better relative to the club.

questions.question_text:
The table shows Ari's marks in three subjects, with the class mean and standard deviation for each.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc} \text{Subject} & \text{Mark} & \mu & \sigma \\ \hline \text{Physics} & 70 & 64 & 8 \\ \text{Chemistry} & 58 & 52 & 5 \\ \text{Biology} & 83 & 74 & 15 \end{array}$
In which subject was his relative performance the best?

options.text: Chemistry
Biology
options.why: Chooses the highest raw mark, $83$, but it comes from the test with by far the largest spread.

options.text: Physics
options.why: Chooses the subject whose raw difference from the mean is second largest, without dividing by each standard deviation.

options.text: All three were equally good.
options.why: The three z-scores are $0.75$, $1.2$ and $0.6$, so the relative performances are clearly different.

questions.solution_text:
Physics: $z = \dfrac{70 - 64}{8} = 0.75$
Chemistry: $z = \dfrac{58 - 52}{5} = 1.2$
Biology: $z = \dfrac{83 - 74}{15} = 0.6$
$1.2$ is the highest of the three $z$-scores, so his relative performance was best in Chemistry, his lowest raw mark.

questions.question_text:
Tom's standardised score in Design was $1.2$.
In Textiles the mean is $66$ and the standard deviation is $7.5$.
What Textiles mark would represent an equivalent performance?

options.why: Subtracted $z\sigma$ from the mean even though the z-score is positive.
Added the z-score itself to the mean instead of multiplying it by the standard deviation first.
Stopped at $z\sigma = 1.2 \times 7.5$ and forgot to add the mean.

questions.solution_text:
An equivalent performance needs the same $z$-score of $1.2$.
$x = \mu + z\sigma$
$= 66 + 1.2 \times 7.5$
$= 66 + 9$
$= 75$

questions.question_text:
Ivy scored $84$ in Test A, where the mean was $76$ and the standard deviation was $16$.
She scored $61$ in Test B, where the mean was $55$ and the standard deviation was $8$.
Ivy says Test A was her stronger result relative to the class.
Is she correct?

options.text: No, because her Test B $z$-score of $0.75$ is higher than her Test A $z$-score of $0.5$
Yes, because $84$ is the higher mark
options.why: Compares raw marks from two tests with different means and spreads.

options.text: Yes, because she is $8$ marks above the mean in Test A but only $6$ marks above in Test B
options.why: Compares the raw differences without dividing by each standard deviation.

options.text: It cannot be decided without knowing how many students sat each test
options.why: The z-score already measures position relative to the group; the group size is not needed.

questions.solution_text:
Test A: $z = \dfrac{84 - 76}{16}$
$= 0.5$
Test B: $z = \dfrac{61 - 55}{8}$
$= 0.75$
$0.75 > 0.5$, so Test B was her stronger result relative to the class and Ivy is not correct.

questions.question_text:
Noah scored $44$ in French, where the mean was $52$ and the standard deviation was $10$.
He scored $39$ in German, where the mean was $51$ and the standard deviation was $8$.
In which subject was his result better relative to the class?

options.text: French, because its $z$-score of $-0.8$ is greater than the German $z$-score of $-1.5$
German, because $-1.5$ is further from zero than $-0.8$
options.why: Compares the sizes of the z-scores and ignores their signs; further below the mean is worse, not better.

options.text: German, because a more negative $z$-score is always the better one
options.why: Applies the lower-is-better rule, which belongs only to contexts such as times where a small raw value is good.

options.text: Neither, because both marks are below the mean so the two results are equally poor
options.why: Treats 'below the mean' as one category instead of measuring how far below in standard deviations.

questions.solution_text:
French: $z = \dfrac{44 - 52}{10}$
$= -0.8$
German: $z = \dfrac{39 - 51}{8}$
$= -1.5$
Both results are below the mean, but $-0.8 > -1.5$, so his French result was better relative to the class.

questions.question_text:
The table shows Rosa's marks in three subjects, with the class mean and standard deviation for each.
$\begin{array}{c|ccc} \text{Subject} & \text{Mark} & \mu & \sigma \\ \hline \text{Maths} & 57 & 63 & 12 \\ \text{English} & 71 & 65 & 8 \\ \text{Science} & 48 & 54 & 4 \end{array}$
In which subject was her relative performance the weakest?

options.text: Science
Maths
options.why: Both Maths and Science are $6$ marks below their means, and this choice ignores that Science has the much smaller standard deviation.

options.text: English
options.why: English is the only subject above its mean, with a z-score of $0.75$, so it is her strongest rather than her weakest.

options.text: Maths and Science equally, since both marks are $6$ below the mean
options.why: Compares the raw differences without dividing by each standard deviation.

questions.solution_text:
Maths: $z = \dfrac{57 - 63}{12} = -0.5$
English: $z = \dfrac{71 - 65}{8} = 0.75$
Science: $z = \dfrac{48 - 54}{4} = -1.5$
$-1.5$ is the lowest of the three $z$-scores, so her relative performance was weakest in Science.

questions.question_text:
Ella scored $69$ in Test 1, where the mean was $60$ and the standard deviation was $6$.
Test 2 has a mean of $72$ and a standard deviation of $10$.
What mark in Test 2 would give Ella the same performance relative to the class?

options.why: Subtracted $z\sigma$ from the mean even though the z-score is positive.
Added the z-score itself to the mean instead of multiplying it by the standard deviation first.
Used Test 1's standard deviation of $6$ with Test 2's mean, instead of Test 2's standard deviation of $10$.

questions.solution_text:
Test 1: $z = \dfrac{69 - 60}{6}$
$= 1.5$
The same relative performance in Test 2 needs the same $z$-score.
$x = \mu + z\sigma$
$= 72 + 1.5 \times 10$
$= 72 + 15$
$= 87$
